subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Look carefully at the world around you. The iron in a farmer's hoe near the Jubba River, the gold dug from mines in the East African highlands, the carbon in a bag of charcoal, the oxygen you are breathing in this very moment, the salt on your family's table, and the calcium in your own bones and in the limestone rocks along the coast — every single one of these is built from tiny building blocks called atoms. In this unit you will discover that the entire universe, from the smallest grain of sand to the largest star, is made from just over one hundred basic substances called elements.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Use symbols and formulae to represent scientific ideas.

cambridge.alignmentStatus: Proposed from unit outcomes — Cambridge sign-off pending
cambridge.alignmentNote: Atoms, elements, compounds and metals versus non-metals are Stage 7 in 0893 (7Cm.01-7Cm.04, 7Cp.05), and the structure and trends of the Periodic Table are Stage 9 (9Cm.01, 9Cp.01). Stage 8 carries none of this unit's chemistry, so only its use of chemical symbols and formulae is claimed.

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 0893 — Stage 8 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Explain what an atom is and describe it as the smallest part of an element.
Define an element and explain why there are only around 118 of them.
Read and write chemical symbols correctly, using capital and lowercase letters properly.
Describe how the Periodic Table is arranged into groups (columns) and periods (rows).
Tell metals apart from non-metals by their properties, with local examples of each.
Describe the properties of some important groups, such as Group 1, Group 7 and Group 0.
Explain the difference between an element, a compound and a mixture.
Read and understand simple chemical formulae such as H2O, CO2 and NaCl.
Describe what happens in a chemical reaction, using the words reactant and product.

concepts.title: Atoms: The Building Blocks of Everything
concepts.explanation:
Imagine you take a small piece of pure gold — perhaps a tiny nugget from a mine in the East African highlands — and you cut it in half. Then you cut one of those halves in half again. Suppose you had a magical knife and could keep cutting, again and again, into smaller and smaller pieces. Would you ever reach a piece so small that it could not be cut any further and still be gold? The answer is yes. That smallest possible piece of gold is called an atom of gold.

An atom is the smallest particle of a substance that still behaves as that substance. Atoms are unimaginably tiny. If you lined up ordinary atoms side by side, it would take around ten million of them just to stretch across the width of a single human hair. They are far too small to see with any ordinary microscope. Yet every object you have ever touched — the camel's leather saddle, the metal cup, the water you drink, your own body — is built from countless billions upon billions of these tiny atoms.

Here is the wonderful part. There are not billions of different kinds of atom. There are only about one hundred and eighteen different kinds. Each different kind of atom makes a different element. Just as the twenty-something letters of an alphabet can be arranged to write every word in a whole language, these hundred or so kinds of atom combine in different ways to build every material in the entire universe. That is a breathtaking economy of design.

Did You Know? The word 'atom' comes from an ancient Greek word, atomos, which means 'cannot be cut'. The idea that everything is made of tiny uncuttable pieces was first suggested more than two thousand years ago, long before anyone could prove it. It took until the last two hundred years for science to show the ancient thinkers were right.

An element is a pure substance that is made of only one type of atom. Because it contains just one kind of atom, an element cannot be broken down into any simpler substance by ordinary chemistry. This is what makes elements the true building blocks of chemistry.

Think about the oxygen you are breathing right now. Oxygen is an element: it is made entirely of oxygen atoms and nothing else. Iron, the metal in a farmer's hoe or a cooking pot, is an element: it is made entirely of iron atoms. Carbon, the black material in the charcoal your family may use for cooking, is an element made only of carbon atoms. Gold, copper, sodium, calcium — each of these is a pure element with its own single type of atom.
concepts.example: Scientists have found around ninety elements occurring naturally on Earth and in the stars, and have made a further two dozen or so in special laboratories. That gives the total of about 118 elements. Some, like oxygen, carbon and iron, are extremely common. Others are so rare that only a few atoms have ever been made. Every element has its own name and its own personality — some are soft, some hard, some are gases, some are shiny metals, and a few are so reactive they burst into flame in water.

concepts.title: Chemical Symbols: A Language for the Whole World
concepts.explanation:
Scientists live and work in every country on Earth, speaking hundreds of different languages. A scientist in Mogadishu, one in Nairobi and one in far-away Japan all need to write about the same elements without confusion. To make this possible, every element is given a short code called a chemical symbol. These symbols are the same in every country and every language, so they act as a shared scientific language for the whole world.

A chemical symbol is made of one or two letters. There is a strict and important rule about how the letters are written: the first letter is always a capital (uppercase) letter, and the second letter, if there is one, is always small (lowercase). This rule is not just for neatness — it can completely change the meaning. For example, Co means the element cobalt, but CO (two capitals) means carbon and oxygen joined together as carbon monoxide. One is a shiny metal; the other is a poisonous gas. The way you write the letters really matters.

Many symbols are easy because they come straight from the English name. O is oxygen, H is hydrogen, C is carbon, N is nitrogen, Ca is calcium, and Al is aluminium. But some symbols look strange at first, because they come from the old Latin names that scientists used hundreds of years ago. This is why the symbol for iron is Fe (from the Latin *ferrum*), the symbol for gold is Au (from *aurum*), the symbol for sodium is Na (from *natrium*), and the symbol for lead is Pb (from *plumbum*).

Here are some of the most useful symbols to know. Notice how many of these elements appear in everyday East African life. Learn this table well, because we will use these symbols constantly for the rest of the unit.

The lightest element; joins with oxygen to make water.

Found in charcoal, diamonds, and all living things.

The gas we need to live; about one fifth of the air.

Half of common table salt; from Latin natrium.

The other half of table salt; a green, choking gas on its own.

In bones, teeth, limestone and seashells.

In tools, cooking pots and your own blood; from Latin ferrum.

A reddish metal used in wires and cooking pans; from cuprum.

A precious, shiny metal mined in the region; from aurum.

A light metal used in cooking pots and drink cans.

Needed by plants and by your body; from Latin kalium.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Your own red blood carries oxygen around your body using iron. Each red blood cell contains millions of tiny iron-carrying parts. This is one reason doctors tell people to eat iron-rich foods like meat, beans and dark green leaves — the same element that makes a hoe strong also keeps your blood healthy.

concepts.title: The Periodic Table: Order Out of Variety
concepts.explanation:
With over a hundred elements to keep track of, scientists needed a sensible way to organise them. Imagine a shopkeeper in the Bakaara market with a hundred different goods thrown together in one heap — finding anything would be impossible. A good shopkeeper arranges goods in neat rows and shelves, grouping similar things together. Scientists did exactly the same thing with the elements, and the result is the Periodic Table.

The Periodic Table is a chart in which every element has its own box. The elements are placed in order of how heavy their atoms are, from the lightest (hydrogen) to the heaviest. But they are not just in one long line. They are arranged in rows and columns so that elements with similar properties end up near each other. This arrangement is so useful that it is one of the most important tools in all of science.

The man most remembered for creating it is Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian scientist who published his table in 1869. What made him brilliant was that when the pattern left a gap, he did not force an element into it. Instead he said, 'there must be an element here that nobody has discovered yet,' and he even predicted what it would be like. Years later, those missing elements were found, and they matched his predictions almost exactly. A good pattern in science does not just organise what we know — it can predict what we do not yet know.

There are two directions to read the Periodic Table, and each has its own special name. This is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit, so read carefully.

A group is a vertical column — one that runs from top to bottom. There are eight main groups, numbered 1 to 8 (the last group is often called Group 0). The wonderful thing about groups is that all the elements in the same group behave in a similar way, because their atoms are built in a similar way. This means if you know how one member of a group behaves, you can make a very good guess about the others. Group 1, for example, contains sodium and potassium, which are both soft, reactive metals.

A period is a horizontal row — one that runs from left to right. As you move across a period, the elements change gradually from metals on the left, through some in-between elements, to non-metals on the right. A helpful way to remember the difference: groups go down (like a group of camels walking in a line down a path), and periods go across (like reading a period, or sentence, from left to right).

It also helps to know that the Periodic Table is split roughly into three regions. On the left and middle are the metals — and this is by far the largest part, since most elements are metals. On the right-hand side are the non-metals. And squeezed along the staircase-shaped line between them are a few in-between elements that share some properties of both. So just by knowing where an element sits, you can already predict a great deal about how it will behave. The position tells the story.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The element helium, the gas that makes balloons float, was discovered in the Sun before it was ever found on Earth. Scientists studying sunlight in 1868 noticed a colour that matched no known element, so they named it after the Greek word for the Sun, helios. Only later was helium found here on our own planet.

concepts.title: Metals and Non-metals
concepts.explanation:
The biggest and most useful division among the elements is between metals and non-metals. You already know many metals from daily life: the iron in a cooking pot, the copper in an electrical wire, the aluminium in a drink can, the gold in jewellery. You also know many non-metals: the oxygen and nitrogen in the air, the carbon in charcoal, the sulfur sometimes used in matches. Metals and non-metals behave in almost opposite ways, and learning their properties lets you predict how a material will act.

Metals share a set of properties that make them extremely useful. Let us go through the most important ones, with examples you can find at home.

Shiny when polished. A clean metal spoon or a gold ring gleams in the light. Scientists call this a lustrous surface.

Good conductors of heat. A metal pot heats up quickly on the fire, which is exactly why we cook with metal and not with wood or clay for boiling.

Good conductors of electricity. This is why electrical wires are made from copper — electricity flows through metals easily.

Malleable, meaning they can be hammered into new shapes without shattering. A blacksmith beats hot iron into a blade or a hoe.

Ductile, meaning they can be pulled into long thin wires. Copper can be drawn out into the thin wires inside a phone charger.

Strong and hard, and most have high melting points, so they stay solid even when very hot. This is why tools and machines are made of metal.

Sonorous, meaning they make a ringing sound when struck — think of a metal bell or two spoons tapped together.

Because of this powerful combination of properties, metals are the materials we reach for whenever we need something strong, long-lasting, able to be shaped, or able to carry heat or electricity. Almost every tool, vehicle, wire and machine depends on them.

Non-metals are, in most ways, the opposite of metals. There are fewer of them, but they are just as important — after all, the air you breathe and the charcoal you cook with are non-metals.

Dull, not shiny (with a few exceptions). A lump of charcoal or a piece of sulfur has no gleam.

Poor conductors of heat and electricity. They are called insulators. This is why the handle of a good cooking pot is often plastic or wood — non-metal materials that do not carry the heat to your hand.

Brittle when solid, meaning they crack or shatter if you hit them, instead of bending. Charcoal crumbles rather than flattens.

Low melting points, and many are gases at ordinary temperatures, such as oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine.

Not sonorous — they make a dull thud, not a ring, when struck.

Lower density, so a piece of a non-metal usually feels lighter than a piece of metal of the same size.

There is one famous exception worth remembering. Carbon in the form of graphite (the 'lead' in a pencil) is a non-metal, yet it does conduct electricity. Nature always keeps a few surprises, and good scientists watch out for exceptions rather than ignoring them.

Did You Know? Mercury is the only metal that is a liquid at room temperature — it flows like shiny silver water. And bromine is one of the very few non-metals that is a liquid too. Most metals are hard solids and most non-metals are gases or brittle solids, but these two break the usual pattern. Mercury is poisonous, so it must never be touched.

Because elements in the same group behave alike, chemists have given special names to some of the most important groups. You do not need to memorise every detail, but knowing these makes the Periodic Table come alive.

Group 1 — the alkali metals. These are soft, light metals such as sodium and potassium. They are so reactive that they must be kept under oil, because they burst into flame if they touch water. This may surprise you, because you eat sodium every day — but only after it has safely joined with chlorine to make harmless table salt. On its own, pure sodium is dangerous.

Group 7 — the halogens. These are colourful, reactive non-metals such as chlorine and iodine. Chlorine is a green, choking gas that is poisonous on its own, yet in tiny amounts it is added to drinking water to kill germs and keep people healthy. Iodine is added to salt in many countries to prevent illness. The same element can be dangerous or life-saving depending on how it is used.
concepts.example: Group 0 (or Group 8) — the noble gases. These are gases such as helium, neon and argon. They are famous for being extremely unreactive — they hardly ever join with anything else. Because helium is lighter than air and does not catch fire, it is used to fill balloons and airships. Because neon glows brightly when electricity passes through it, it is used in the bright signs of city shops.

concepts.title: Compounds, Mixtures and Formulae
concepts.explanation:
So far we have talked about pure elements. But most of the materials around you are not pure elements at all — they are elements joined together. When atoms of different elements join chemically, they make a brand new substance called a compound. This is one of the most important ideas in chemistry, so let us build it up slowly and carefully.

The clearest example is water. Water is not an element. It is a compound made from two elements: hydrogen and oxygen, chemically joined. On their own, hydrogen and oxygen are both invisible gases — and hydrogen even burns fiercely. Yet when their atoms join in the right way, they make water, a cool liquid that puts out fire. This is the astonishing thing about compounds: the compound is completely different from the elements that made it.

Another example is right on your dinner table. Common salt is a compound called sodium chloride, made from the element sodium (a dangerous, reactive metal) joined with the element chlorine (a poisonous green gas). Neither is safe to eat on its own, yet joined together they make the harmless salt that flavours your food and that the sea leaves behind when it dries on the coast. The calcium in limestone and seashells is likewise joined with carbon and oxygen to make a compound called calcium carbonate.

It is very important not to confuse a compound with a mixture. In a compound, the elements are chemically joined, and it takes a chemical reaction to separate them. The compound has new properties, quite unlike its ingredients. In a mixture, the substances are simply mixed together without joining chemically, so each one keeps its own properties and they can usually be separated easily.

For example, air is a mixture of oxygen, nitrogen and other gases — they are jumbled together but not joined, and each keeps its own nature. Sea water is a mixture of water and salt; when the sun dries it on the coast, the salt is left behind, showing the two were never chemically joined. But water itself is a compound, because its hydrogen and oxygen are truly joined and cannot be separated just by drying or filtering.

Scientists describe a compound using a formula — a short code made of chemical symbols and small numbers. Once you learn to read a formula, it tells you exactly which atoms are inside and how many of each. This is one of the most useful skills in chemistry.

The symbols tell you which elements are present. The small number written just after and below a symbol tells you how many atoms of that element there are. If a symbol has no number, it means there is just one atom. Look carefully at these examples:

H2O (water) means 2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen joined together.

CO2 (carbon dioxide) means 1 atom of carbon and 2 atoms of oxygen. This is the gas you breathe out.

NaCl (common salt) means 1 atom of sodium (Na) and 1 atom of chlorine (Cl).

CaCO3 (calcium carbonate, in limestone) means 1 calcium, 1 carbon and 3 oxygen atoms.
concepts.example: So a formula is like a recipe written in code. Just as a recipe for canjeero tells you how much of each ingredient to use, a formula tells you exactly how many atoms of each element are combined in the compound. Reading formulae carefully — noticing exactly where each small number sits — is a skill worth practising until it feels natural.

concepts.title: An Introduction to Chemical Reactions
concepts.explanation:
How do compounds get made in the first place? And how does iron turn to rust, or charcoal turn to ash and heat? The answer is a chemical reaction. A chemical reaction is a change in which one or more substances are turned into one or more new substances. This is different from simply mixing or melting, because in a chemical reaction the atoms rearrange themselves to make something genuinely new.

Scientists use two special words to describe a reaction. The substances you start with are called the reactants. The new substances you end with are called the products. We can show a reaction as a kind of sentence, with an arrow that means 'turns into':

Let us look at a reaction you have almost certainly seen: rusting. When a farmer leaves an iron hoe out in the damp air, it slowly turns orange-brown and crumbly. This is a chemical reaction. The iron joins with oxygen from the air to make a new substance, iron oxide, which we call rust. We can write it like this:

Here iron and oxygen are the reactants, and rust is the product. Notice that rust is completely different from the shiny, strong iron we started with — it is weak, flaky and orange. That is the sign of a chemical reaction: a new substance with new properties has appeared, and you cannot simply turn it back by drying or cooling it.

Another everyday example is burning charcoal. When your family lights charcoal to cook, the carbon in the charcoal joins with oxygen in the air to make carbon dioxide gas, and releases heat and light in the process. We write it as carbon + oxygen -> carbon dioxide. The carbon and oxygen are the reactants; the carbon dioxide is the product. The heat that cooks your food is the energy released by this reaction.
concepts.example: Did You Know? When you cook bread or canjeero, chemical reactions are hard at work. Heat causes reactions that make new substances, giving cooked food its brown colour and delicious smell. The raw batter and the finished bread are chemically different — which is why you cannot un-cook a loaf. Cooking is one of the oldest kinds of chemistry humans ever practised.

methods.title: Sorting Materials into Metals and Non-metals
methods.example: To collect objects from around your home and sort them into metals and non-metals by testing their properties.
steps: Draw a table with two columns: Metal and Non-metal.
Take each object in turn. Look at it — is it shiny or dull?
Gently tap it against a hard surface — does it make a ringing sound or a dull thud?
Feel it — is it cold and hard (many metals feel cold) or not?
Decide whether it is a metal or a non-metal, and write it in the correct column with your reason.

methods.title: Testing for Metals with a Magnet
methods.example: To find out which metals in your home are magnetic, and to learn that being magnetic is a special property of only a few metals, not all of them.
steps: Lay out all your objects on a table.
Bring the magnet slowly near each object in turn.
Notice whether the object is attracted (pulled towards the magnet) or not attracted.
Record your result for each object.
Sort your results into two groups: magnetic and not magnetic.

methods.title: A Chemical Reaction with Vinegar and Limestone
methods.example: To observe a chemical reaction between an acid (vinegar) and a compound containing calcium (chalk, limestone, or an eggshell), and to spot the signs that a reaction has taken place.
steps: Place the crushed eggshell or piece of chalk in the clear glass.
Pour a little vinegar over it, just enough to cover it.
Watch very closely for the first few minutes. Look for bubbles or fizzing.
Listen carefully — can you hear a soft fizzing sound?
Record everything you observe, and note how long the fizzing lasts.

methods.title: Watching Rust Form (A Slow Chemical Reaction)
methods.example: To observe the slow chemical reaction of rusting, and to find out what conditions make iron rust faster.
steps: Put one nail in a dry jar with nothing else. This nail has air but no water.
Put the second nail in a jar and cover it completely with water, then add a thin layer of oil on top to keep air out. This nail has water but little air.
Put the third nail in a jar with just enough water to half-cover it, so it has both air and water.
Leave all three jars in a safe place and look at them once a day for four or five days.
Each day, record which nails are rusting and how much.

workedExamples.title: Counting Atoms in a Formula
workedExamples.prompt: Learning to count the atoms in a formula is one of the most useful skills in this unit. Let us work through some examples together, showing every step, so you can see exactly how it is done. Remember the two rules: a symbol with no number means one atom, and a small number after a symbol tells you how many atoms of that element there are.
workedExamples.solution:
Example 1: How many atoms are in H2O (water)?

Look at each symbol in turn. The first is H (hydrogen), and just after it is a small 2. So there are 2 hydrogen atoms.

The next symbol is O (oxygen), with no number after it. So there is 1 oxygen atom.

Add them up: 2 + 1 = 3 atoms in total, made of 2 elements.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: The smallest particle of an element is called an: (a) molecule (b) atom (c) compound (d) mixture
workedExamples.solution: (b) atom. An atom is the smallest particle of an element that still behaves as that element.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: About how many different elements are there? (a) 12 (b) 50 (c) 118 (d) 1000
workedExamples.solution: (c) 118. There are about 118 known elements, around 90 of them found naturally.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: The chemical symbol for iron is: (a) Ir (b) In (c) Fe (d) Fr
workedExamples.solution: (c) Fe. The symbol for iron comes from the Latin word ferrum.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: The chemical symbol for sodium is: (a) So (b) Sd (c) Na (d) S
workedExamples.solution: (c) Na. The symbol for sodium comes from the Latin word natrium.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: A vertical column in the Periodic Table is called a: (a) period (b) group (c) row (d) kingdom
workedExamples.solution: (b) group. A group is a vertical column; a period is a horizontal row.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a property of most metals? (a) dull (b) brittle (c) good conductor of electricity (d) a gas
workedExamples.solution: (c) good conductor of electricity. Metals conduct electricity well; the other options describe non-metals.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a non-metal? (a) iron (b) copper (c) oxygen (d) gold
workedExamples.solution: (c) oxygen. Oxygen is a non-metal gas. Iron, copper and gold are all metals.

activities.title: Sorting Materials into Metals and Non-metals
activities.materials: A notebook and pencil; About ten safe objects: a metal spoon, a coin, an aluminium can, a copper wire, a piece of charcoal, a plastic cup, a wooden spoon, a stone, a piece of chalk or limestone, a rubber band
steps: Draw a table with two columns: Metal and Non-metal.
Take each object in turn. Look at it — is it shiny or dull?
Gently tap it against a hard surface — does it make a ringing sound or a dull thud?
Feel it — is it cold and hard (many metals feel cold) or not?
Decide whether it is a metal or a non-metal, and write it in the correct column with your reason.

activities.title: Testing for Metals with a Magnet
activities.materials: A magnet (a fridge magnet works well); A collection of metal and non-metal objects: an iron nail, a steel spoon, an aluminium can, a copper coin or wire, a gold or brass item if you have one, a plastic item, a piece of wood
steps: Lay out all your objects on a table.
Bring the magnet slowly near each object in turn.
Notice whether the object is attracted (pulled towards the magnet) or not attracted.
Record your result for each object.
Sort your results into two groups: magnetic and not magnetic.

Safety: Magnets must never go in or near your mouth — swallowing magnets is a medical emergency. Keep them away from babies and young children. Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards.

activities.title: A Chemical Reaction with Vinegar and Limestone
activities.materials: A small amount of vinegar (a household acid); A clean, crushed eggshell, or a small piece of chalk or limestone (all contain calcium carbonate, CaCO3); A clear glass or jar; A spoon
steps: Place the crushed eggshell or piece of chalk in the clear glass.
Pour a little vinegar over it, just enough to cover it.
Watch very closely for the first few minutes. Look for bubbles or fizzing.
Listen carefully — can you hear a soft fizzing sound?
Record everything you observe, and note how long the fizzing lasts.
Safety: Only test safe kitchen liquids such as lemon juice and vinegar. Never touch or mix cleaning products like bleach, and never taste anything you are testing.

activities.title: Watching Rust Form (A Slow Chemical Reaction)
activities.materials: Three similar iron nails (steel nails work well); Three clear jars or cups; Water, and a little cooking oil; A notebook to record daily observations over several days
steps: Put one nail in a dry jar with nothing else. This nail has air but no water.
Put the second nail in a jar and cover it completely with water, then add a thin layer of oil on top to keep air out. This nail has water but little air.
Put the third nail in a jar with just enough water to half-cover it, so it has both air and water.
Leave all three jars in a safe place and look at them once a day for four or five days.
Each day, record which nails are rusting and how much.
Safety: Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards.

activities.title: Observe: Compounds, Mixtures and Formulae
activities.materials: A notebook and pencil; About ten safe objects: a metal spoon, a coin, an aluminium can, a copper wire, a piece of charcoal, a plastic cup, a wooden spoon, a stone, a piece of chalk or limestone, a rubber band
steps: Look for an example of compounds, mixtures and formulae around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words H2O and CO2.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

realProblems.prompt: A blacksmith near Kismaayo hammers a hot piece of iron into a hoe without it shattering. Which property of metals makes this possible, and what is the name for that property?
realProblems.answer: The metal can be hammered into shape without shattering because it is malleable. This property lets a blacksmith shape hot iron into tools.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — H2O, CO2, NaCl — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: The metal can be hammered into shape without shattering because it is malleable. This property lets a blacksmith shape hot iron into tools.

realProblems.prompt: Amina notices that the salt left behind when sea water dries on the coast can be separated from the water easily. Does this make sea water a compound or a mixture? Explain.
realProblems.answer: It is a mixture, because the salt and water are not chemically joined and can be separated easily (the water dries away and leaves the salt behind).
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — H2O, CO2, NaCl — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: It is a mixture, because the salt and water are not chemically joined and can be separated easily (the water dries away and leaves the salt behind).

realProblems.prompt: A farmer's iron gate rusts faster on the side facing the sea than the side facing inland. Using what you know about rusting, suggest why.
realProblems.answer: Salt in the sea air speeds up rusting, so the side facing the sea meets more salty, moist air and rusts faster. Rusting needs iron, oxygen and water, and salt makes it happen more quickly.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — H2O, CO2, NaCl — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Salt in the sea air speeds up rusting, so the side facing the sea meets more salty, moist air and rusts faster. Rusting needs iron, oxygen and water, and salt makes it happen more quickly.

realProblems.prompt: Table salt is safe to eat, yet it is made from a dangerous metal and a poisonous gas. Explain how this is possible, using the words element and compound.
realProblems.answer: Table salt is a compound (sodium chloride). The dangerous element sodium and the poisonous element chlorine are chemically joined, and the compound has completely new, safe properties — unlike the elements it is made from.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — H2O, CO2, NaCl — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Table salt is a compound (sodium chloride). The dangerous element sodium and the poisonous element chlorine are chemically joined, and the compound has completely new, safe properties — unlike the elements it is made from.

realProblems.prompt: A cook lights charcoal to prepare food. Name the two reactants and the one product of the burning reaction, and say what useful thing the reaction gives off.
realProblems.answer: The reactants are carbon (in the charcoal) and oxygen (from the air); the product is carbon dioxide. The reaction also gives off heat (and light), which cooks the food.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — H2O, CO2, NaCl — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: The reactants are carbon (in the charcoal) and oxygen (from the air); the product is carbon dioxide. The reaction also gives off heat (and light), which cooks the food.

realProblems.prompt: Mendeleev left gaps in his Periodic Table for elements that had not yet been discovered, and predicted their properties. Explain why this is such a powerful example of how a good scientific pattern works.
realProblems.answer: Mendeleev's gaps show that a good pattern does more than organise what we already know — it can predict what we do not yet know. Because the elements he predicted were later found with the properties he described, it proved the pattern was real and deeply true about nature.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between an atom and an element.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: An atom is the smallest single particle of an element. An element is a pure substance made of many atoms of the same kind. For example, iron is an element, and a single iron atom is an atom.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: State three properties of metals and three properties of non-metals.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Oxygen = O; carbon = C; iron = Fe; gold = Au; sodium = Na.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a group and a period in the Periodic Table?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Metals: shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (bendable), strong, high melting point (any three). Non-metals: dull, poor conductors (insulators), brittle, low melting point, often gases (any three).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between a compound and a mixture, giving one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A group is a vertical column of the Periodic Table, and elements in it behave alike. A period is a horizontal row, across which elements change from metal to non-metal.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: How many atoms of each element are in the formula CaCO3? How many atoms in total?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: In a compound the elements are chemically joined and make a new substance (e.g. water). In a mixture they are only mixed and keep their own properties (e.g. air).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Define the words reactant and product, using rusting as your example.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: CaCO3 has 1 calcium, 1 carbon and 3 oxygen atoms. That is 5 atoms in total.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to:
I can explain what an atom is and describe it as the smallest part of an element.
I can define an element and explain why there are only around 118 of them.
I can read and write chemical symbols correctly, using capital and lowercase letters properly.
I can describe how the Periodic Table is arranged into groups (columns) and periods (rows).
I can tell metals apart from non-metals by their properties, with local examples of each.
I can describe the properties of some important groups, such as Group 1, Group 7 and Group 0.
I can explain the difference between an element, a compound and a mixture.
